{{Short description|Probability problem}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Hamburger [[moment problem]]''', named after [[Hans Hamburger|Hans Ludwig Hamburger]], is formulated as follows: given a [[sequence]] {{math|(''m''<sub>0</sub>, ''m''<sub>1</sub>, ''m''<sub>2</sub>, ...)}}, does there exist a positive [[Borel measure]] {{mvar|μ}} (for instance, the measure determined by the [[cumulative distribution function]] of a [[random variable]]) on the [[real line]] such that

:<math>m_n = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x^n\,d\mu(x)</math>?

In other words, an affirmative answer to the problem means that {{math|(''m''<sub>0</sub>, ''m''<sub>1</sub>, ''m''<sub>2</sub>, ...)}} is the sequence of [[moment (mathematics)|moments]] of some positive Borel measure {{mvar|μ}}.

The [[Stieltjes moment problem]], [[Vorobyev moment problem]], and the [[Hausdorff moment problem]] are similar but replace the real line by <math>[0,+\infty)</math> (Stieltjes and Vorobyev; but Vorobyev formulates the problem in the terms of matrix theory), or a [[bounded interval]] (Hausdorff).

== Characterization ==

The Hamburger moment problem is solvable (that is, {{math|(''m''<sub>''n''</sub>)}} is a sequence of [[moment (mathematics)|moments]]) if and only if the corresponding [[Hankel matrix|Hankel kernel]] on the nonnegative [[integer]]s

:<math>
A =
\left(\begin{matrix}
m_0 & m_1 & m_2 & \cdots     \\
m_1 & m_2 & m_3 & \cdots  \\
m_2 & m_3 & m_4 & \cdots  \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots
\end{matrix}\right)</math>

is [[positive definite kernel|positive definite]], i.e.,

:<math> \sum_{j,k\ge0}m_{j+k}c_j\overline{c_k}\ge0 </math>

for every arbitrary sequence {{math|(''c''<sub>''j''</sub>)<sub>''j'' ≥ 0</sub>}} of [[complex number]]s that are finitary (i.e., {{math|''c<sub>j</sub>'' {{=}} 0}} except for finitely many values of {{mvar|j}}).

For the "only if" part of the claims simply note that

:<math> \sum_{j,k\ge0}m_{j+k}c_j \overline{c_k} = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \left|\sum_{j\geq 0} c_j x^j\right|^2\,d \mu(x) </math>,

which is non-negative if <math> \mu </math> is non-negative.

We sketch an argument for the converse. Let {{math|'''Z'''<sup>+</sup>}} be the nonnegative integers and {{math|''F''<sub>0</sub>('''Z'''<sup>+</sup>)}} denote the family of complex valued sequences with finitary support.  The positive Hankel kernel {{mvar|A}} induces a (possibly degenerate) [[sesquilinear]] product on the family of complex-valued sequences with finite support.  This in turn gives a [[Hilbert space]]

:<math>(\mathcal{H}, \langle\; , \; \rangle)</math>

whose typical element is an [[equivalence class]] denoted by {{math|[''f'']}}.

Let {{mvar|e<sub>n</sub>}} be the element in {{math|F<sub>0</sub>('''Z'''<sup>+</sup>)}} defined by {{math|''e<sub>n</sub>''(''m'') {{=}} [[Kronecker delta|''δ'']]<sub>''nm''</sub>}}. One notices that

:<math>\langle [e_{n+1}], [e_m] \rangle = A_{m,n+1} = m_{m+n+1} = \langle [e_n], [e_{m+1}]\rangle</math>.

Therefore, the [[shift operator]] {{mvar|T}} on <math>\mathcal{H}</math>, with {{math|''T''[''e<sub>n</sub>''] {{=}} [''e''<sub>''n''&nbsp;+ 1</sub>]}}, is [[symmetric operator|symmetric]].

On the other hand, the desired expression

:<math>m_n = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x^n\,d \mu(x)</math>
 
suggests that {{mvar|μ}} is the [[spectral measure]] of a [[self-adjoint operator]]. (More precisely stated, {{mvar|μ}} is the spectral measure for an operator <math>\overline{T}</math> defined below and the vector [1], {{harv|Reed|Simon|1975|p=145}}).  If we can find a "function model" such that the symmetric operator {{mvar|T}} is [[multiplication operator|multiplication by {{mvar|x}}]], then the spectral resolution of a [[extensions of symmetric operators|self-adjoint extension]] of {{mvar|T}} proves the claim.

A function model is given by the natural isomorphism from ''F''<sub>0</sub>('''Z'''<sup>+</sup>) to the family of [[polynomial]]s, in one single real variable and complex coefficients: for ''n''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0, identify ''e<sub>n</sub>'' with ''x<sup>n</sup>''. In the model, the operator ''T'' is multiplication by ''x'' and a densely defined symmetric operator. It can be shown that ''T'' always has self-adjoint extensions. Let <math>\overline{T}</math> be one of them and ''μ'' be its spectral measure. So

:<math>\langle \overline{T}^n [1], [1] \rangle = \int x^n d \mu(x)</math>.

On the other hand,

:<math> \langle \overline{T}^n [1], [1] \rangle =  \langle T^n [e_0], [e_0] \rangle = m_n</math>.

For an alternative proof of the existence that only uses [[Riemann–Stieltjes_integral|Stieltjes integrals]], see also,{{sfn|Chihara|1978|p=56}} in particular theorem 3.2.  

=== Uniqueness of solutions ===

The solutions form a convex set, so the problem has either infinitely many solutions or a unique solution.

Consider the {{math|(''n'' + 1) × (''n'' + 1)}} [[Hankel matrix]]

:<math>\Delta_n = \left[\begin{matrix}
m_0 & m_1 & m_2 & \cdots & m_{n}    \\
m_1 & m_2 & m_3 & \cdots & m_{n+1} \\
m_2 & m_3 & m_4 & \cdots & m_{n+2} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
m_{n} & m_{n+1} & m_{n+2} & \cdots & m_{2n}
\end{matrix}\right]</math>.

Positivity of {{mvar|A}} means that, for each {{mvar|n}}, {{math|det(Δ<sub>''n''</sub>) ≥ 0}}. If {{math|det(Δ<sub>''n''</sub>) {{=}} 0}}, for some {{mvar|n}}, then

:<math>(\mathcal{H}, \langle \; , \; \rangle)</math>

is finite-dimensional and {{mvar|T}} is self-adjoint. So in this case the solution to the Hamburger moment problem is unique and {{mvar|μ}}, being the spectral measure of {{mvar|T}}, has finite support.

More generally, the solution is unique if there are constants {{mvar|C}} and {{mvar|D}} such that, for all {{mvar|n}}, {{math|{{abs|''m''<sub>''n''</sub>}} ≤ ''CD''<sup>''n''</sup>''n''!}} {{harv|Reed|Simon|1975|p=205}}. This follows from the more general [[Carleman's condition]].

There are examples where the solution is not unique; see e.g.{{sfn|Chihara|1978|p=73}}

== Polynomials ==
The Hamburger moment problem is intimately related to [[orthogonal polynomials]] on the real line. That is, assume <math>\{m_{n}\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}_{0}}</math> is the moment sequence of some positive measure <math>\mu</math> on <math>\mathbb{R}</math>. Then for any polynomial
<math display="block">p(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} a_j x^j \in \mathbb{R},</math> 
it holds that
<math display="block">\int p(x)^2 d\mu = \int\left( \sum_{j,k=0}^{n} a_j a_k x^{j+k} \right) d\mu = \sum_{j,k=0}^{n} a_j a_k m_{j+k} \geq 0, \quad \forall n\in \mathbb{N}_{0},</math> 
such that the Hankel matrix is positive semidefinite. This is a necessary condition for a sequence to be a moment sequence and a sufficient condition for the existence of a positive measure.{{sfn|Schmüdgen|2017|p=2}}

The [[Gram–Schmidt]] procedure gives a basis of orthogonal polynomials in which the operator: <math>\overline{T}</math> has a tridiagonal ''Jacobi matrix representation''.  This in turn leads to a ''tridiagonal model'' of positive Hankel kernels.

An explicit calculation of the [[Cayley transform]] of {{mvar|T}} shows the connection with what is called the ''[[Nevanlinna class]]'' of analytic functions on the left half plane.  Passing to the non-commutative setting, this motivates ''Krein's formula'' which parametrizes the extensions of partial isometries.

The cumulative distribution function and the probability density function can often be found by applying the inverse [[Laplace transform]] to the moment generating function
:<math>m(t) = \sum_{n=0}m_n\frac{t^n}{n!}</math>,
provided that this function converges.
